paragraphs: The paper asks how causality can be given a precise mathematical foundation. Its starting point is that describing what happens probabilistically and describing what happens after an intervention are closely connected tasks. The authors therefore propose extending the measure-theoretic foundations of probability, rather than treating causal reasoning as a separate mathematical subject.

Their central object is a causal space. It combines an ordinary probability space with a collection of transition probability kernels, which they call causal kernels. The probability space describes uncertainty, while the additional kernels encode causal information. This makes the causal component an explicit part of the mathematical structure instead of leaving it implicit in a probabilistic description.

The contribution is a proposed foundational framework grounded in measure theory. The authors argue that it also clarifies longstanding difficulties involving cycles, hidden variables, and stochastic processes. These are presented as areas where the framework sheds light on existing limitations, rather than as evidence that a universally accepted or final axiomatisation of causality has been achieved.
neurips-2023-a-measure-theoretic-axiomat.tldr: The paper proposes a measure-theoretic foundation for causality by augmenting probability spaces with kernels that encode causal information.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to bound a neural network's error when its test data differ from its training data and test labels are unavailable. Existing approaches can produce bounds that say little in practice, or estimates that look accurate on average while substantially understating error for many shifts. The authors aim for an informative upper bound with more dependable coverage.

Their bound uses disagreement between classifiers and is inspired by an existing divergence-based approach, while being easier to evaluate and tighter. Computing it requires training one multiclass classifier to disagree with another. The authors introduce a theoretically justified disagreement loss that performs better in practice than previously used proxy objectives.

The guarantee depends on a condition that the authors report holds effectively all the time in practice; it is therefore qualified rather than unconditional. Across natural and synthetic shift benchmarks, the method produces valid, informative error bounds. Its average estimation accuracy is comparable to, but does not exceed, competitive baselines, so the contribution centers on dependable upper bounds rather than superior average prediction of error.
neurips-2023-almost-provable-error-bound.tldr: A disagreement-based method gives informative error upper bounds under distribution shift, subject to a condition reported to hold consistently in practice.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning has transferred successfully from images to graphs, but this paper asks whether the same ingredients explain its success in both settings. Through a systematic study, the authors find that several components commonly associated with visual contrastive learning play different roles when the underlying model is a graph neural network.

The reported observations have distinct scopes. Positive samples are not always required for graph contrastive learning. Negative samples can be unnecessary for graph classification, and also for node classification when particular normalization modules are used. Data augmentation appears less influential than in visual methods: even simple, domain-independent transformations such as Gaussian noise can achieve fairly good performance.

The authors provide theoretical insight by examining the implicit preferences built into graph neural network architectures. Their explanation connects those architectural properties to the observed behavior of contrastive methods. The practical implication is that graph learning methods should account for what the architecture already contributes, rather than assume that every component inherited from image-based contrastive learning is equally important.
neurips-2023-architecture-matters-uncove.tldr: Graph neural network architecture helps explain why graph contrastive learning can work without some ingredients commonly used in visual contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Sharing observations can improve what multiple agents perceive, but their messages may describe different moments. Communication delays, interruptions, and misaligned clocks make this unavoidable in practice. If objects move between those moments, combining the messages directly can place information at incompatible locations and undermine the benefit of collaboration.

CoBEVFlow addresses this mismatch by compensating for motion in a bird's-eye view of the scene. Its BEV flow assigns a motion vector to each spatial location, allowing perceptual features from asynchronous messages to be moved to appropriate positions. It handles irregular, continuous timestamps without discretizing them. Because it transports existing features rather than synthesizing replacements, the approach avoids additional noise associated with generating new features.

The authors also introduce IRV2V, a synthetic dataset designed to represent different forms of temporal asynchrony. Experiments on that dataset and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset show consistent improvements over the compared baselines, including robustness under extreme asynchrony. These findings support motion-based alignment as a way to preserve the usefulness of delayed collaborative information.
neurips-2023-asynchrony-robust-collabora.tldr: CoBEVFlow aligns delayed collaborative observations by moving existing bird's-eye-view features according to estimated scene motion.

paragraphs: Distributed learning must sometimes remain reliable despite Byzantine attacks. Much of the existing understanding concerns training problems expressed as minimization. The paper focuses on a broader setting: variational inequalities, which also cover formulations such as min-max problems that arise in modern machine learning and distributed training.

This distinction matters because methods and guarantees for ordinary minimization do not automatically address these other formulations. The authors develop several methods with provable Byzantine robustness specifically for distributed variational inequalities. They also analyze convergence, connecting the proposed defenses to guarantees about how the methods progress toward a solution.

The work extends a research direction that the abstract describes as previously addressed by only one study. The authors report removing limitations of that earlier work and provide numerical comparisons supporting their theoretical findings. The contribution therefore combines additional robust algorithms, convergence analysis, and computational evidence. Its significance is to broaden the mathematical settings in which distributed learning can be studied under Byzantine attacks, beyond the better-understood case of minimization.
neurips-2023-byzantine-tolerant-methods-.tldr: The paper develops provably Byzantine-robust methods for distributed variational inequalities and supports their convergence theory with numerical comparisons.

paragraphs: Highly accurate vision models can be difficult to compress without sacrificing the accuracy that makes them valuable. CAP tackles this problem through unstructured pruning, which removes individual model weights. Its central idea is to account for complex relationships among weights while deciding what to remove, rather than treating those relationships as incidental to compression.

The framework combines a theoretically justified pruning method with an efficient fine-tuning procedure that recovers performance after compression. Experiments cover Vision Transformers, modern convolutional networks, and architectures combining the two. The authors report examples with at least 75% sparsity and no more than a 1% relative accuracy drop, demonstrating that substantial weight removal can preserve much of these models' performance.

CAP is also compatible with structured pruning and quantization, and the authors report practical speedups of 1.5 to 2.4 times without accuracy loss. Separately, they show that large, highly accurate models trained through self-supervision can tolerate moderate sparsity with negligible accuracy loss. The reported compression levels and benefits apply to the demonstrated settings rather than every possible vision model.
neurips-2023-cap-correlation-aware-pruni.tldr: CAP uses weight correlations and recovery fine-tuning to prune modern vision models substantially while preserving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training an energy-based model by maximum likelihood typically requires sampling, often through Langevin dynamics. Starting that sampling from noise can make it difficult to explore the model effectively. A generator can supply better starting points, but replacing sampling with generation can introduce bias, and a generator trained only to match the energy model misses direct guidance from observed data.

The paper proposes jointly learning the energy-based model and its complementary generator through interwoven maximum-likelihood procedures. The generator learns to match both the energy model and the empirical data distribution. This gives it a richer source of information for producing the initial states used by the energy model's sampling process.

Learning the generator from observations introduces another inference problem: determining its latent variables. The framework handles this with a second MCMC process, initialized by a separate inference model. These three models are connected through two sampling-based teaching processes, giving the method its dual-MCMC name. The authors present this integration as a way to make energy-based learning effective and efficient while addressing the generator bias they identify.
neurips-2023-learning-energy-based-model.tldr: Dual-MCMC teaching jointly trains an energy model, a generator, and an inference model so observed data can improve the generator used to initialize sampling.

paragraphs: LLaVA-Med addresses the gap between general-purpose vision-language assistants and the specialized vocabulary and imagery used in biomedical research. The authors adapt an existing general-domain model to answer open-ended questions about biomedical images. Their approach draws on a broad collection of figures and captions extracted from PubMed Central.

Training follows a curriculum with two stages. First, figure-caption pairs help align biomedical vocabulary with visual content. Next, instruction-following examples generated by GPT-4 from the captions teach the model to respond conversationally to open-ended requests. The progression separates acquiring domain vocabulary from learning how to use that knowledge in a dialogue.

The authors report completing training in less than 15 hours using eight A100 GPUs. They describe strong multimodal conversational behavior and evaluate the model on three standard biomedical visual question-answering datasets. It exceeds the previous supervised state of the art on certain metrics, a narrower finding than outperforming prior systems on every measure. The contribution shows how existing biomedical image-caption material can support relatively efficient adaptation of a conversational vision-language model.
neurips-2023-llava-med-training-a-large-.tldr: LLaVA-Med adapts a general vision-language model through biomedical captions and generated instructions, improving certain biomedical question-answering metrics after under 15 hours of training.

paragraphs: Averaging neural network weights can improve generalization, but the paper identifies a weakness in approaches that average points along one training trajectory only after training ends. Those networks may lack enough functional diversity for averaging to deliver its full benefit. Lookaround builds diversification and averaging into the optimization process itself.

Each iteration begins from a shared set of weights and trains several networks using different data augmentations. This is the around step. The average step then combines their weights, and that average becomes the common starting point for the next iteration. The two steps aim to maintain both diversity in what the networks do and proximity in their weights.

The authors argue that this combination is essential for effective weight averaging and leads to flatter minima with better generalization. They provide convergence analysis and experiments on benchmarks including CIFAR and ImageNet, using both convolutional networks and Vision Transformers. The reported improvements over competing methods support repeated exploration and recombination during training as an effective optimization strategy.
neurips-2023-lookaround-optimizer-k-step.tldr: Lookaround repeatedly trains networks from shared weights with different augmentations, then averages them to promote diversity, flatter minima, and better generalization.

paragraphs: Image deraining networks can perform well on laboratory benchmarks yet struggle on real-world images. A common response is to train with richer, more complex backgrounds, expecting that greater variety will improve generalization. The authors systematically investigate this idea and find that, in their experiments, increasing background complexity instead encourages overfitting to particular rain degradations.

Their explanation is that the network tends to learn whichever elements of the background and degradation are least complex and most useful for reducing training loss. With sufficiently complex backgrounds, learning specific rain patterns becomes an attractive shortcut. When backgrounds are simpler than the rain streaks, the network instead prioritizes reconstructing the background, reducing its tendency to specialize in those rain patterns.

The experiments show that simplifying training backgrounds can improve deraining generalization. This makes the relative complexity of image content and corruption a meaningful training consideration, rather than assuming that more complicated content is always beneficial. The authors also present this explanation as a promising perspective for understanding generalization in other low-level vision tasks.
neurips-2023-networks-are-slacking-off-u.tldr: Experiments suggest that simpler training backgrounds can improve deraining generalization by shifting learning away from memorizing specific rain patterns.

paragraphs: One way to apply graph learning to tabular data is to connect nearby examples and treat each row as a node. Such nearest-neighbor graphs often link examples with similar labels, which can make them appear naturally useful for classification. This paper examines whether that constructed structure actually adds value when no graph was originally present.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for class distributions in nearest-neighbor graphs. They analyze Cross-Class Neighborhood Similarity, a measure used to assess the usefulness of graph structure, and study how distinguishable classes become when deep graph networks operate on a k-nearest-neighbor graph. This connects the graph construction to the class information available to the resulting model.

In their quantitative experiments under full supervision, using a k-nearest-neighbor graph provides no benefit over a baseline that ignores structure. Qualitative results suggest the framework estimates neighborhood similarity well and hint at a broader lack of usefulness in that setting. That broader conclusion remains suggestive, while the findings motivate investigating alternative graph construction methods.
neurips-2023-on-class-distributions-indu.tldr: Theory and experiments question the value of k-nearest-neighbor graphs for fully supervised tabular classification, with no gains over a structure-agnostic baseline in the reported tests.

paragraphs: Probabilistic principal component analysis reduces data to a lower-dimensional representation, but its widespread use has outpaced theoretical guarantees for its maximum-likelihood estimates. A central obstacle is rotational ambiguity: different parameter settings related by rotation can describe the same model. Recovering one uniquely designated parameter setting is therefore not the appropriate target.

The authors address this by using quotient spaces, which treat rotationally equivalent parameter settings as the same object. In an appropriate quotient Euclidean space, they prove consistency of the maximum-likelihood solution. This expresses recovery in a way that respects the model's symmetry rather than demanding a distinction that the model itself cannot identify.

The consistency results also cover a broader family of estimators beyond maximum likelihood. Under an additional compactness assumption, the authors establish strong consistency for the maximum-likelihood estimate and corresponding strong covariance estimation. The contribution is a mathematical justification for estimation in PPCA, with the stronger result explicitly tied to that assumption and the basic recovery claim formulated around rotational equivalence.
neurips-2023-on-the-consistency-of-maxim.tldr: The paper proves consistency for PPCA estimation by treating rotationally equivalent parameters as identical, with stronger guarantees under a compactness assumption.

paragraphs: Data valuation methods assign value to individual examples to help assess their quality and influence on learning. Many such methods exist, but comparing them meaningfully requires shared datasets, models, and evaluation procedures. OpenDataVal supplies that common environment so researchers and practitioners can examine which valuation methods help with their intended uses.

The framework brings together image, language, and tabular datasets with implementations of eleven data valuation algorithms. Its prediction-model interface supports importing models from scikit-learn. The authors also define four downstream machine learning tasks for assessing the quality of assigned data values, tying evaluation to what those values enable a user to accomplish.

Benchmarking with this framework finds that no algorithm is uniformly best across all evaluated tasks. The implication is that choosing a valuation method should depend on the downstream objective, rather than on an expectation of one universally superior score. Public documentation and a leaderboard support applying the framework and comparing new algorithms within the same evaluation environment.
neurips-2023-opendataval-a-unified-bench.tldr: OpenDataVal standardizes comparisons of data valuation algorithms and finds that the best choice depends on the downstream task.

paragraphs: Earlier findings linked better object recognition in neural networks with better predictions of responses in the brain's inferotemporal visual cortex. That relationship suggested that improving recognition accuracy could also improve models of biological vision. This paper revisits the expectation after major increases in network scale and visual-task performance.

Across three independent experiments, the authors find the opposite trend: networks with higher ImageNet accuracy have become worse predictors of inferotemporal responses. Spatially resolved recordings of neuronal activity help investigate the discrepancy. The analysis indicates that ImageNet-trained networks rely on visual features different from those represented in this brain region, with the mismatch worsening as recognition accuracy increases.

The authors address the mismatch using the neural harmonizer, a training routine that aligns learned representations with humans. Their results suggest that harmonized networks can escape the observed trade-off between ImageNet accuracy and neural prediction. The findings motivate revising task-performance-only approaches to modeling visual cortex and incorporating additional biological constraints, including human psychophysics, into model development.
neurips-2023-performance-optimized-deep-.tldr: Higher ImageNet accuracy coincides with worse inferotemporal response prediction in the reported experiments, while human-aligned training suggests a way to overcome the trade-off.

paragraphs: Federated frequency estimation lets multiple clients jointly estimate how often data values occur while limiting what the coordinating server can see. The setting studied here requires secure summation: the server receives only the sum of vectors held by clients. The paper asks how estimation can improve when communication is allowed to occur over multiple rounds.

For a single round, count sketch is already known to be nearly optimal in an information-theoretic sense. The authors propose a different sketch algorithm for multiple rounds and prove that it is more accurate than a naive extension of count sketch. They also show that both approaches can achieve better accuracy when the particular estimation problem is simpler.

This dependence on problem difficulty motivates a two-phase procedure that allows smaller sketches for easier instances. The authors additionally provide mechanisms for making their algorithm differentially private and evaluate their methods on real datasets. The contribution combines improved multi-round estimation with adaptation to instance difficulty, while explicitly accommodating the server's restricted access to client information.
neurips-2023-private-federated-frequency.tldr: The paper improves multi-round federated frequency estimation with a new sketch algorithm and adapts sketch size to problem difficulty while supporting differential privacy.

paragraphs: Natural behavior becomes difficult to predict as one looks further into the future. Representations learned in constrained tasks may therefore fail to capture the dynamics of freely behaving animals. This paper develops a self-supervised, multi-task approach intended to represent behavior across both short and long timescales.

The method combines two components. An action-prediction objective targets the distribution of actions over future timesteps, accommodating the uncertainty in what comes next. A multi-scale architecture builds separate latent spaces for short-term and long-term dynamics. Together, these components give the representation distinct ways to capture local behavior and broader patterns without placing both timescales into a single undifferentiated space.

The authors first demonstrate representations of local and global dynamics in robots operating across different environments and terrains. They then apply the method to the MABe 2022 Multi-Agent Behavior challenge, placing first overall on both the mice and fly benchmarks. Across these settings, the reported representations capture multiple factors driving behavior and support a wide range of downstream tasks.
neurips-2023-relax-it-doesnt-matter-how-.tldr: Predicting future action distributions in separate short- and long-term latent spaces produces useful behavior representations and leads both MABe 2022 animal benchmarks.

paragraphs: In-context learning is a striking capability of large language models, but its underlying mechanisms remain difficult to explain. This paper studies an alternative sequence-prediction method, clone-structured causal graphs, that acquires comparable in-context learning capabilities while providing a more interpretable view of how those capabilities arise.

The authors identify three interacting mechanisms in these models. They learn reusable template circuits for completing patterns, retrieve templates appropriate to the current context, and bind unfamiliar tokens to suitable positions within those templates. This account explains how a previously learned pattern can be reused when the particular tokens appearing in a new context have changed.

The paper also gathers evidence for the hypothesis that related mechanisms operate in language models. In both model families, different capabilities emerge at different degrees of overparameterization, suggesting that extra capacity helps learn more complex templates. This supports a possible explanation rather than proving an identical mechanism in transformers. Demonstrating these behaviors with small models and datasets also points toward alternative architectures for studying in-context learning.
neurips-2023-schema-learning-and-rebindi.tldr: Interpretable sequence models exhibit in-context learning through reusable templates and token rebinding, offering evidence for a possible mechanism in language models.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised domain generalization aims to learn from few labels and still perform well in an unseen domain. Many approaches assume that every unlabeled training example and every test example belongs to a known class. This paper addresses the more difficult situation in which those data also contain classes outside the known set.

The proposed CWAEE method separates the work into exploring and exploiting unlabeled data. For exploration, it uses one-versus-rest classifiers together with thresholds adapted to individual classes to detect known and unknown classes. This makes class identification sensitive to differences among classes instead of imposing one shared decision threshold on all of them.

For exploitation, the method applies consistency regularization to augmented samples produced using Fourier Transformation. This component encourages consistent predictions across those transformations to improve generalization to the unseen domain. Experiments on real-world datasets support the method's effectiveness and superiority in the evaluated setting. Its central contribution is to combine class-aware detection with a generalization objective while explicitly accounting for unknown classes in both unlabeled training data and testing.
neurips-2023-semi-supervised-domain-gene.tldr: CWAEE combines class-specific detection thresholds with Fourier-based consistency training to generalize across domains when unlabeled data include unknown classes.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a common formulation for minimization, saddle-point, and fixed-point problems. As these problems grow, distributing computation becomes useful, but communication between participating machines can dominate the cost. This paper targets that bottleneck by combining three established ways of reducing communication demands within one approach.

The three ingredients exploit similarity among local functions, compress the information sent between machines, and perform local updates. They address both how often machines need to communicate and how much information each exchange requires. The authors present their combination as a previously unavailable joint approach for variational inequalities, saddle problems, and even minimization.

The proposed methods come with theoretical communication-complexity guarantees that the authors report as the best for the distributed variational inequality methods considered. Experiments in adversarial learning, using synthetic and real datasets, support the theoretical results. The significance lies in coordinating the three sources of efficiency: communication can be reduced through the relationship among local problems, the representation of messages, and the amount of work performed locally.
neurips-2023-similarity-compression-and-.tldr: The paper combines local-function similarity, compressed messages, and local updates to improve communication guarantees for distributed variational inequalities.

paragraphs: Distinguishing and outlining surgical instruments is difficult because instruments vary and can be hard to differentiate. This paper reformulates instrument segmentation as a task guided by text prompts. The goal is to use language to support a more nuanced understanding of instruments and make the model more adaptable to new instrument types.

The model starts with pretrained image and text encoders. A mask decoder combines attention-based and convolution-based prompting schemes to produce segmentation predictions. Rather than relying on one description per instrument, a mixture-of-prompts mechanism uses multiple prompts. The authors also introduce a hard instrument area reinforcement module to improve understanding of image features and the precision of the resulting masks.

Experiments across several surgical instrument segmentation datasets show superior performance and promising generalization. These results support using language as an active input to segmentation, with multiple descriptions contributing to improved predictions. The authors describe the approach as, to their knowledge, the first promptable implementation for this task and point to its potential in robotic-assisted surgery.
neurips-2023-text-promptable-surgical-in.tldr: A vision-language model uses multiple text prompts and a specialized mask decoder to improve surgical instrument segmentation across evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a shared explanation for two observations about larger neural networks: loss often decreases according to a power law, while particular capabilities can appear suddenly. Its starting hypothesis is that knowledge and skills are acquired in discrete units, called quanta. Scaling then changes which of these units a model has learned.

The authors derive a relationship between the frequency of those units and the overall scaling curve. If units are learned from most frequently used to least frequently used, a power-law distribution of use frequencies explains power-law loss scaling. They validate this prediction on toy datasets before investigating how language-model behavior can be decomposed into skills.

For language models, they use gradients to automatically identify a diverse collection of candidate quanta. They tentatively find that the frequency of their use roughly follows a power law aligned with the observed language-model scaling exponent. That language-model evidence remains qualified, while the framework provides a concrete hypothesis linking gradual aggregate improvement to the acquisition of discrete capabilities.
neurips-2023-the-quantization-model-of-n.tldr: The Quantization Model explains scaling through discrete skills learned by frequency, with toy-data validation and tentative supporting evidence from language models.

paragraphs: Training a large model independently requires substantial time and resources. This paper asks whether organizations could benefit from exchanging parts of models instead of producing every component themselves. The proposed goods are sets of learned weights, and the authors investigate what would be needed to make trading those parameters a viable activity.

The work develops a framework containing infrastructure for market operations, studies strategies for exchanging parameters, and proposes ways for participants to monetize them. Advances in aligning and interpolating models motivate the possibility of such exchanges. The focus is therefore broader than combining models: it includes the operational and strategic questions involved when separate participants trade components.

The authors show that mutual gains are possible relative to participants training isolated models from scratch, even when the setting is competitive. This is an existence claim about beneficial market participation, rather than a guarantee that every exchange benefits everyone. The findings suggest parameter markets as a possible future approach to improving large-scale training by making others' learned contributions available through trade.
neurips-2023-train-n-trade-foundations-o.tldr: The paper develops foundations for trading model weights and shows that participants can mutually benefit compared with training isolated models from scratch.

paragraphs: Hedonic games model how agents form groups according to individual preferences. A core-stable grouping permits no subset of agents that would prefer to leave and form its own coalition. Such groupings often fail to exist, and finding one can be computationally difficult even when it does exist.

The paper relaxes this requirement by allowing at most an epsilon fraction of all possible coalitions to block the proposed grouping. For Simple Fractional and Anonymous hedonic games, the authors design efficient algorithms producing partitions whose permitted blocking fraction decreases exponentially with the number of agents. This offers a tractable form of stability without requiring the complete absence of dissatisfied coalitions.

The definition also has a probabilistic interpretation: a uniformly sampled coalition has only a small chance of blocking. The authors extend this viewpoint to more complex sampling distributions and situations where valuations must be learned from samples. They establish both positive and negative results about which distributions permit efficient computation of approximately stable outcomes with arbitrarily high confidence.
neurips-2023-varepsilon-fractional-core-.tldr: Allowing a small fraction of blocking coalitions enables efficient stability guarantees for two classes of hedonic games, with further results for learned preferences.

paragraphs: A common explanation for graph neural network performance is homophily: connected nodes tend to share labels. Another explanation emphasizes similar neighborhood patterns among nodes of the same class. This paper argues that either account is incomplete unless it also considers how different those nodes are from nodes in other classes.

The authors propose that a favorable representation has less variation within classes than separation between classes. They develop a contextual stochastic block model and two measures of node distinguishability to investigate this relationship. The analysis examines graph filters, node-degree distributions, and class variances, and identifies a mid-homophily pitfall that occurs widely in graph datasets.

Experiments on real tasks link the advantage of graph neural networks to both within-class and between-class distinguishability across homophily levels. Building on this observation, the authors introduce a nonlinear, feature-based metric using hypothesis testing and a statistical threshold. In synthetic and real-world benchmark experiments, it reveals advantages and disadvantages of graph-aware models more effectively than existing homophily measures.
neurips-2023-when-do-graph-neural-networ.tldr: The paper explains GNN usefulness through both within-class similarity and between-class separation, producing a metric that outperforms homophily measures in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Adapting a large pretrained model can require substantial computation even when only a small number of parameters are learned. InCA attaches lightweight cross-attention modules to intermediate activations of a frozen base model. These adapters survey representations already inside the network to identify which ones are useful for a downstream task.

Because adapter training is isolated from the base model, many adapters can be trained efficiently in parallel. On ViT-L/16, an adapter containing 1.3% as many parameters as the full model matches full fine-tuning accuracy on average across eleven classification tasks. The average qualification matters: the reported result does not assert an exact match on every task.

The authors also adapt a ViT-G/14 model with more than 1.8 billion parameters using over twenty parallel adapters on one V100 GPU, reporting a 76% reduction in GPU memory use. Learned adapters can be modified incrementally or combined for flexible learning settings. The method also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ImageNet-to-Sketch multi-task benchmark, supporting the usefulness of accessible intermediate representations.
neurips-2023-your-representations-are-in.tldr: InCA trains lightweight cross-attention adapters over frozen intermediate representations, enabling parallel adaptation and matching full fine-tuning accuracy on average in one reported evaluation.
